                    <title>Hydrogen production from seawater: Low-cost catalyst could cut energy use and resist corrosion</title>
                    <description>Using a range of advanced characterization techniques, researchers say they have developed a novel method with the potential to produce hydrogen from seawater using a process that requires less energy, resists corrosion and could support more economical hydrogen production.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hydrogen-production-seawater-catalyst-energy.html</link>

                    <title>New research finds frequent disease outbreaks in B.C. salmon farms, endangering wild salmon</title>
                    <description>A new study with unprecedented access to Atlantic salmon farms in British Columbia raises urgent questions about the federal government's approach to regulating salmon farms and highlights disease risk to wild salmon populations.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-frequent-disease-outbreaks-bc-salmon.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Botanists comb Gabon's rich rainforests with nature on the line</title>
                    <description>Each year, Gabon's lush rainforests yield the discovery of previously unknown plant species to botanists like Archange Boupoya—who believes that this exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth needs to be cataloged to be saved.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-botanists-gabon-rich-rainforests-nature.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>What is 'human composting'—and how does it work?</title>
                    <description>What should happen to your body after you die? It's hardly a topic you'd bring up over dinner, but it's a decision that will eventually need to be made, either by you or by those you leave behind.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-human-composting.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Scientists produce less disruptive research as they age, but their breakthroughs are more likely to last</title>
                    <description>Science often advances in small steps, with researchers gradually building on previous discoveries. But every now and then, a breakthrough comes along that challenges conventional thinking and changes the direction of a field.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-scientists-disruptive-age-breakthroughs.html</link>
                    <category>Education</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:30:06 EDT</pubDate>

                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Hidden chromosome structures reveal greater complexity in how roundworms organize DNA</title>
                    <description>Almost every cell in our body contains around two meters (6.6 feet) of DNA, packed into a tiny nucleus. Yet for the cell to function, this enormous amount of genetic material must remain organized and accessible. Researchers at the University of Basel have now discovered three distinct types of large chromosomal domains that help organize DNA in nuclei.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hidden-chromosome-reveal-greater-complexity.html</link>
                    <category>Molecular & Computational biology</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:20:07 EDT</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news712244581</guid>

                                    </item>

                    <description>I never thought my shoelaces would get stolen.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-power-poop-conservationists-animal-scat.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Ancestors all around—millions of dead people linger in Americans' memories</title>
                    <description>Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints' Day, All Souls' Day and the Day of the Dead. But deceased loved ones don't disappear from people's social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancestors-millions-dead-people-linger.html</link>
                    <category>Social Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:10:01 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>AI-powered robotic laboratory paves the way for discovering next-generation heat-resistant coatings</title>
                    <description>Researchers have developed a self-driving laboratory that combines artificial intelligence and robotics to automate laboratory tasks, from accurately measuring and mixing chemical ingredients to high-temperature furnace processing and sample retrieval.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ai-powered-robotic-laboratory-paves.html</link>
                    <category>Materials Science</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:09:12 EDT</pubDate>

                            <item>
                    <title>Two distinct sleep stages emerge in jumping spider, including a REM-like state</title>
                    <description>Humans and other vertebrates go through various stages of sleep, including REM (rapid eye movement) sleep characterized by rapid eye movements and muscle twitches. Can a similar sleep state be observed in spiders? Researchers from the Institute of Organismic Biology at the University of Bonn investigated this in the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata. The work is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-distinct-stages-emerge-spider-rem.html</link>
                    <category>Plants & Animals</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:00:17 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Audit reveals suspected fabricated references across physics, chemistry, engineering and computing journals</title>
                    <description>Months after a Columbia University School of Nursing–led audit published in the Lancet reported thousands of fabricated citations in medical papers, the same research team has found the same problem in the physical sciences, engineering and computing.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-reveals-fabricated-physics-chemistry-journals.html</link>
                    <category>Education</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:00:01 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Protecting isn't enough—creating integrated conservation landscapes is key</title>
                    <description>New Monash University research has revealed how countries could strengthen their conservation networks by looking beyond the boundaries of national parks and protected areas—and focusing on how these areas connect.</description>

                    <title>How shoes change our bones—and what that tells us about the evolution of walking</title>
                    <description>We tend to think of our bones as solid, unchanging support structures inside our bodies, but a recent study from the University of Chicago shows just how much they can change depending on how we use them.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-bones-evolution.html</link>
                    <category>Evolution</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:20:12 EDT</pubDate>

                            <item>
                    <title>Biodiversity is a priority for European municipalities</title>
                    <description>As urbanization spreads worldwide, the loss and fragmentation of habitats are driving the global decline in biodiversity. At the same time, urban green spaces like parks, meadows and forests have the potential to contribute significantly to biodiversity conservation at the local and regional levels.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-biodiversity-priority-european-municipalities.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Climate change exposes gaps in Europe's protected-area network</title>
                    <description>As the climate changes, protecting wildlife increasingly depends on both the conditions within protected areas and the connections between them. A new study published in Conservation Letters identifies where climatic stability and opportunities for movement coincide in Europe, and where gaps could undermine conservation.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-climate-exposes-gaps-europe-area.html</link>
                    <category>Environment</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 14:00:02 EDT</pubDate>

                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Interfacial intelligence: A new way to design polymer brushes</title>
                    <description>Polymer brushes are dense layers of polymer chains that can be engineered to change how a surface interacts with its surroundings. By controlling interactions with water, ions, proteins and other materials, they can reduce friction, prevent unwanted materials from sticking, improve separation and support the functionality of sensors and other devices.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-interfacial-intelligence-polymer.html</link>
                    <category>Polymers</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:40:01 EDT</pubDate>

                    <title>Fractional calculus helps 1D model mimic correlations seen in 2D phase transitions</title>
                    <description>Phase transitions are strongly constrained by spatial dimension. In conventional one-dimensional systems with short-range interactions, thermal fluctuations generally prevent continuous degrees of freedom from maintaining order over long distances.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-fractional-calculus-1d-mimic-2d.html</link>

                    <title>Clouds on a lava planet challenge what astronomers expected</title>
                    <description>A rocky lava planet once thought to be too extreme to have an atmosphere appears to be wrapped in one with a reflective layer of vaporized silicate mineral clouds, the same family of compounds that make up quartz and sand.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-clouds-lava-planet-astronomers.html</link>
                    <category>Planetary Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:20:01 EDT</pubDate>

                            <item>
                    <title>Emotional content can improve how people process conversations</title>
                    <description>New in JNeurosci, Pyry Heikkinen and colleagues, from the University of Helsinki, explored how emotional meaning influences the way the human brain prioritizes information during naturally spoken conversations in a cocktail party setting.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-emotional-content-people-conversations.html</link>

                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Laser-blasted plasma shows how instabilities could heat the sun's corona</title>
                    <description>From its visible surface, the sun radiates heat at a relatively cool temperature of 5,800 Kelvin. Yet within the thin outer layer of the sun's atmosphere known as the corona, electrons can reach temperatures of millions of degrees, for reasons astronomers have yet to fully explain.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-laser-blasted-plasma-instabilities-sun.html</link>
                    <category>Astronomy</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 13:00:10 EDT</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news712234865</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/laser-blasted-plasma-s.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>World-famous or local legend? New study investigates global and local forms of collective memory and group identity</title>
                    <description>Napoleon Bonaparte and Bernardo O'Higgins: two 19th-century military leaders renowned to this day in their native countries of France and Chile. Yet, while Napoleon's name and exploits are known throughout the world, O'Higgins remains largely obscure outside his homeland. This phenomenon demonstrates the distinction between global and local collective memory—the shared knowledge of the past that shapes group identity—and it is the topic of newly published research from Constructor University's Professor Dr. Mariana Macedo together with Dr. Melanie Oyarzun, Professor Dr. Cristian Candia and Professor Dr. César A. Hidalgo.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-world-famous-local-legend-global.html</link>
                    <category>Social Sciences</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 12:50:06 EDT</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news712225893</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/napoleon.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Lizard tail preserved in amber sheds light on a 100-million-year-old defense mechanism</title>
                    <description>A lizard making a dramatic escape, leaving its tail wriggling behind as it darts to safety, is an image familiar to many. Tail-shedding is one of the most widespread defenses against predators among living lizards, yet tracing the origins of this extraordinary ability has proved to be surprisingly difficult—how can we tell when this escape tactic first arose in lizards?</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-lizard-tail-amber-million-year.html</link>
                    <category>Evolution</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 12:40:06 EDT</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news712234861</guid>
                                            <media:thumbnail url="https://scx1.b-cdn.net/csz/news/tmb/2026/lizard-tail-preserved.jpg" width="90" height="90" />
                                    </item>
                            <item>
                    <title>Solving an ancient cold case: Roman was brutally murdered</title>
                    <description>This 2,000-year-old cold case offered a wealth of information, Leiden archaeologists Carol van Driel-Murray and Mark Driessen explain. Few skeletons from the late Iron Age and early Roman era have been preserved, making this largely intact skeleton a valuable research resource. In their new book Victims of Violence from the Early Roman Fort Velsen, Van Driel-Murray and Driessen reconstruct the cause of this man's death. This interdisciplinary study combined archaeological, historical and forensic insights.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-ancient-cold-case-roman-brutally.html</link>
                    <category>Archaeology</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 12:30:01 EDT</pubDate>
                    <guid isPermaLink="false">news712224823</guid>

                    <title>Britain's 1972 school reform may have lowered dementia diagnoses half a century later</title>
                    <description>A new study provides perhaps the strongest evidence yet that education can help mitigate long-term dementia risk.</description>

                    <title>Japan's largest marine DNA study detects 126 fish species farther north than previously recorded</title>
                    <description>As climate change reshapes habitats both on land and at sea, you might go to the beach one day, only to find yourself in a place that looks nothing like you remember, around sea creatures you don't recognize.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-japan-largest-marine-dna-fish.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Armored amphibian lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago, fossils suggest</title>
                    <description>Scientists report fossil evidence of the first fully marine amphibian in a study from the University of California, Davis; Peking University; and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. The amphibian is an armored, giant salamander–sized, bottom-dwelling ocean creature that the researchers named Gerrothorax maritimus.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-armored-amphibian-sea-million-years.html</link>

                            <item>
                    <title>Physicists reveal new paradigm for fiber growth in neurodegenerative diseases</title>
                    <description>Some proteins that are linked to neurodegenerative diseases can form both liquid droplets and amyloid fibers. But how are these two states connected, and where do the fibers grow? Leiden physicists Liru Feng and Louise Jawerth have discovered a counter-intuitive mechanism.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-physicists-reveal-paradigm-fiber-growth.html</link>

                    <title>An American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?</title>
                    <description>A U.S. startup has booked two Indian rocket launches to test a planned service no company has sold before: sunlight at night.</description>

                            <item>
                    <title>Mapping the hidden global labor powering AI</title>
                    <description>Most people know by now that artificial intelligence powers much of the online world, sifting through social media posts, planning driving routes or helping to choose a movie to watch. But what goes largely unseen is the human labor—often performed by people working for low wages in the Global South—that makes this careful algorithmic lifestyle curation possible.</description>
                    <link>https://phys.org/news/2026-10-hidden-global-labor-powering-ai.html</link>
                    <category>Economics & Business</category>                    <pubDate>Mon, 26 Oct 2026 11:30:01 EDT</pubDate>
